children.note: Before the reasons, know what we mean by a record. It is just written proof of what happened to your money.

children.topic: A record: a note of money
children.note: Any note that says what money came in or went out, when, how much and why. It can be in a book, on a phone or on paper slips.

manas.q: What is a record, in simple words?

children.note: Cash, M-Pesa or bank money that you receive, such as sales, fares or wages.

manas.q: What does "money in" mean?

children.note: Money you pay away, such as stock, fuel, rent, school fees or food.

manas.q: What does "money out" mean?

children.note: Bookkeeping is the daily habit of writing down money in and money out. Accounting then uses those notes to tell you how the business is doing.

manas.q: What is bookkeeping?

children.note: Most people forget small amounts within a day or two. Small forgotten amounts add up to big holes over a month.
Everyone who handles money: a duka owner, a matatu owner, a salon, a farmer, a boda boda rider and a family running a home.

children.topic: Reason 1: Do I really make money?
children.note: The first reason is to know the truth. Busy days and full hands do not prove a profit.
Profit is what is left after you take away what the business spent to earn the money. If costs are bigger, you made a loss.

manas.q: How do you find profit in the simplest way?

children.topic: Busy is not the same as profitable
children.note: A shop can sell a lot and still lose money if it pays too much for stock or spends on things it does not notice.

children.topic: Know your best and worst items
children.note: Records show which goods sell fast and which ones sit on the shelf. You can then buy more of the good ones.
When you know what an item cost you, you can set a price that leaves something for you.
Keep business money apart from family money. If you mix them, you cannot tell whether the business is earning.

manas.q: Why keep business money separate from home money?

children.note: Records let you check that the money you have is the money you should have.
Start cash + money in − money out = cash you should have. Count the drawer and compare. A gap means a mistake or a loss.

manas.q: How do you work out the cash you should have?

children.topic: Spot a short or extra amount
children.note: Less cash than expected is a shortage. More cash than expected is an overage. Both need checking.

manas.q: What is a cash shortage?

children.note: Your M-Pesa and bank statements are a second record. Compare them with your book to find missing or double entries.
When people know the owner checks the book every day, fewer things go missing.
Records also catch honest mistakes, such as wrong change given or a supplier paid twice.
Banks, SACCOs and microfinance lenders want proof that you can repay.
A lender wants to see steady money coming in. Written records and statements give that proof.

manas.q: Why do lenders want to see your records?

children.note: Many lenders look at several months of sales or statements to judge how much you can repay. Ask your lender exactly what they need.
If records show money left over each month, the lender can see you are able to pay the instalments.
Group lenders also trust members who can show clear records of savings and business income.
Mobile money statements show real payments over time, which can support your loan request.
Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) expects businesses to keep records and issue electronic invoices. Only rules checked today are given here.
Keep business and tax records for five years from the end of the period they relate to. This comes from Section 23 of the Tax Procedures Act 2015. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: How long must you keep business records in Kenya?

children.note: eTIMS is the Electronic Tax Invoice Management System. It is free from KRA and works on a phone or a computer. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: What is eTIMS?

children.topic: Everyone in business must use eTIMS
children.note: All persons in business must sign up and issue electronic tax invoices, whether VAT-registered or not. This includes sole traders and the informal sector. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: Who must issue eTIMS invoices?

children.note: Since 1 January 2024, a business cost can only be claimed for tax if an electronic tax invoice backs it. So ask your suppliers for one. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: Since when must claimed expenses have an eTIMS invoice?

children.note: If the seller is a small business or small farmer with yearly sales not over KES 5 million, the buyer makes the invoice for them on eCitizen (Buyer Initiated Invoicing). (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: What is Buyer Initiated Invoicing?

children.topic: Costs that need no eTIMS invoice
children.note: Some costs are left out, such as salaries and wages, imports, air tickets, interest and bank fees. See the KRA page for the full list. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)
Records from the past help you make better choices for the future.
A budget is a plan of how much money you expect to receive and how you will spend it.

manas.q: What is a budget?

children.note: Records show when sales go up (for example before school opens or festive season) so you can stock up in time.
Knowing your monthly surplus helps you save for rent, school fees, a new motorbike or repairs.
When records show steady profit, you can decide calmly whether to open a second shop or buy a second bike.
You do not need many books. Keep a few simple records every day.
One list of each day's money in and money out. This is the heart of all records.

manas.q: What is the one record every business should keep daily?

children.note: Keep papers or messages that prove each payment or sale. An invoice asks for payment; a receipt proves it was paid.

manas.q: What is the difference between an invoice and a receipt?

children.note: Download or save your statements each month and keep them with your book.
A list of customers who took goods on credit, how much, and when they promised to pay.

manas.q: What is a debtor?

children.note: A list of suppliers you still have to pay, with amounts and due dates.

manas.q: What is a creditor?

children.note: A simple count of goods on the shelf, done weekly or monthly, shows what you have and what is missing.
Note things like a fridge, motorbike or sewing machine: what you paid and when.
Pick the way that is easiest for you. The best system is the one you use every day.
A cheap exercise book with columns: date, details, money in, money out. Total each day.

manas.q: What columns does a simple cash book need?

children.note: A spreadsheet on a phone can add up totals for you. Keep a backup copy.
Many apps record sales and costs and give a daily summary. Check the cost and that your data is backed up.
Taking payments through a till leaves an automatic record of each sale.

children.topic: A box or file for papers
children.note: Put receipts and invoices in a labelled envelope or file for each month so you can find them later.
Record each amount on the day it happens. Waiting a week means guessing.
Old records still matter for tax, loans and disputes.
Records for a period ending 31 December 2025 should be kept until at least 31 December 2030 (2025 + 5). (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)
Store books away from water, fire and rats. Take phone photos of important papers as a backup.
Save copies to a second place, such as an email or cloud folder, in case the phone is lost.
Real numbers using only adding and taking away.
Money in from sales: KES 42,500. The question is how much is left after costs.
Stock 28,000 + rent 3,500 + electricity 1,200 + transport 1,800 = KES 34,500.
42,500 − 34,500 = KES 8,000 left for the week. Without the book she would only be guessing.

children.topic: Otieno the boda boda rider: one day
children.note: Fares received: KES 2,400. He also bought lunch for KES 200.
Fuel 900 + small repair 300 = KES 1,200. Profit = 2,400 − 1,200 = KES 1,200.
Lunch is personal, not a bike cost. After lunch he has 1,200 − 200 = KES 1,000 to take home.
Morning cash KES 2,000, sales KES 15,300, paid out KES 4,800. Counted at night: KES 11,900.
12,500 − 11,900 = KES 600 short. Now check the book, M-Pesa and change given.
Total = KES 240,000. Average = 240,000 ÷ 6 = KES 40,000 a month.
She buys 120 sodas at KES 50 each and sells at KES 65 each.
Income KES 45,000. Spending: rent 15,000, food 12,000, school 6,000, transport 4,500, power and water 3,000.
Spent = KES 40,500. Left to save = 45,000 − 40,500 = KES 4,500.
These habits make records useless. Avoid them from day one.
Taking shop cash for home needs without writing it down hides the real profit.
KES 50 here and 100 there can add up to thousands each month.
Filling the book at the end of the week leads to guesses and forgotten items.
Without proof you cannot check a supplier, claim a tax cost or settle an argument.
Goods given on credit and not written down are often never paid for.
Keep records for the five years KRA asks for, not just until the end of the month. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)
Try these, then open the answer steps.
Money in: 3,200, 2,900, 3,500. Money out: 2,100, 1,800, 2,600. What is the profit?
Start 1,500, sales 8,700, paid out 2,300. Counted 7,400. Short or over?
Records for the year ending 31 December 2025: when may you stop keeping them?
Not before 31 December 2030, which is five years after the period ends. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

nodeData.topic: Money in, money out: a cash book
nodeData.note: A cash book lists every shilling coming in and going out, with a balance after each line. Learn to keep one for cash, M-Pesa and bank, and to check it against the drawer every evening.

children.note: A cash book is one simple list of every shilling that comes into the business and every shilling that goes out, day by day. It builds on topic 1: once you know why records matter, this is the first record to keep.
Every line is either money coming in (a sale, a loan, money you put in) or money going out (stock, rent, wages). Nothing else goes in a cash book.

manas.q: What two kinds of entry does a cash book have?

children.note: It tells you, every evening, how much money you should have. Without it you cannot tell a good day from a lost or stolen shilling.
It is not a list of credit sales or debts owed to you. It only records money that has actually moved — cash, M-Pesa or bank.
Accountants call the cash book a 'book of prime entry', meaning the first place a transaction is written down before anything else.

manas.q: Why is the cash book called a book of prime entry?

children.note: A school exercise book works fine. A phone notes app or a simple spreadsheet also works. What matters is writing every day.

children.topic: The parts of a cash book
children.note: Each page has the same few columns. Learn these and you can read any cash book.
The day the money moved. Write it on every line so you can find things later.
A few words saying what it was: 'Cash sales', 'Paid Baraka Bakers for bread', 'Rent for November'. Short but clear.

manas.q: What goes in the Details column?

children.note: The amount received. Only received money goes here.

manas.q: What goes in the Money in column?

children.note: The amount paid. Only paid money goes here.

manas.q: What goes in the Money out column?

children.note: How much money you have after this line. It is worked out line by line, so you always know where you stand.
A small column for the receipt or M-Pesa code. It links the line to its proof (more in topic 3).
Balance just means 'how much is left'. There are three you must know: opening, running and closing.
The money you start the day or week with, before any new sale or payment. In a duka this is often the float of small change.

manas.q: What is an opening balance?

children.note: After each line: last balance + money in − money out. It runs down the page so you never have to add everything again.

manas.q: How do you work out a running balance?

children.note: The balance after the last line of the day or week. It is what you should physically have.

manas.q: What is a closing balance?

children.note: The closing balance of today is written as the opening balance of tomorrow. Accountants say it is 'carried down' (c/d) and 'brought down' (b/d).

manas.q: What does "balance carried down" mean?

children.note: Closing balance = Opening balance + Total money in − Total money out. If this does not agree with your running balance, there is a mistake.

manas.q: What is the closing balance formula?

children.note: Money in a Kenyan duka sits in three places. Keep a separate column (or a separate book) for each so each one can be checked.
Cash is counted in the drawer, M-Pesa is checked on the phone statement, bank is checked on the bank statement. Mixing them hides mistakes.

manas.q: Why keep cash, M-Pesa and bank in separate columns?

children.note: Notes and coins in the drawer. This is the one you count with your hands at closing time.
Money received on your till or phone and payments you send from it. The M-Pesa statement shows every movement with a code.
Money in the bank account: deposits, cheques, card payments and transfers. Match it to the bank statement (CA11 · 10).
Banking cash is not a sale. Write money out in the cash column and the same amount money in the bank column.

manas.q: How do you record taking cash to the bank?

children.note: M-Pesa and bank charges are money out. Write them on their own line, or the book will never match the statement.
If you take money for home, write it as money out: 'Owner took for home (drawings)'. It is not a business expense, but it did leave.

manas.q: What are drawings?

children.note: A full Monday–Saturday cash book with three columns. Every balance below has been added up and checked.
Monday morning Mama Wanjiku has cash 3,000 (her float), M-Pesa 5,500 and bank 20,000. Total money: KES 28,500.
Cash sales +6,200; M-Pesa sales +4,800; paid bread and milk supplier in cash −3,500. Balances: cash 5,700 · M-Pesa 10,300 · bank 20,000.
Cash sales +5,400; M-Pesa sales +5,100; paid flour supplier by M-Pesa −7,000. Balances: cash 11,100 · M-Pesa 8,400 · bank 20,000.
Cash sales +4,900; M-Pesa sales +3,600; took 8,000 cash to the bank (cash −8,000, bank +8,000). Balances: cash 8,000 · M-Pesa 12,000 · bank 28,000.
Cash sales +6,000; M-Pesa sales +4,200; rent paid from bank −12,000. Balances: cash 14,000 · M-Pesa 16,200 · bank 16,000.
Cash sales +7,300; M-Pesa sales +6,000; electricity tokens by M-Pesa −1,500; she took 2,000 cash for home (drawings). Balances: cash 19,300 · M-Pesa 20,700 · bank 16,000.
Cash sales +8,100; M-Pesa sales +6,700; paid her helper 3,000 cash; paid sugar and oil supplier by M-Pesa −9,000. Balances: cash 24,400 · M-Pesa 18,400 · bank 16,000.
Next Monday's opening balances are cash 24,400, M-Pesa 18,400, bank 16,000 — total KES 58,800.
Total money rose from 28,500 to 58,800, up 30,300. The 8,000 banking appears as both in and out, so it adds nothing — it is the same money moving.
Every evening count the drawer and compare it with the cash column. This is called a cash count, and it catches mistakes the same day.
Sort notes and coins by size and count each pile. Write down how many of each, then multiply and add.

manas.q: What is a cash count?

children.note: Put the counted total next to the closing balance in the cash column. They should be exactly the same.
Book says 24,400 but the drawer has 24,100. The drawer is 300 short (24,400 − 24,100).

manas.q: What is a cash shortage?

children.note: Look for: change given wrongly, a sale written as cash that was really M-Pesa, a small payment not written down, or a counting slip. Count again first.
If the drawer has more than the book, it is 'cash over'. It usually means a sale was not written down. Find it; do not just pocket it.

manas.q: What does "cash over" mean?

children.note: If you cannot find it, write a line 'Cash short 300' (money out) so the book agrees with reality. Then watch for a pattern.
At day end, check the M-Pesa balance on the phone or statement against the M-Pesa column. Same idea, no counting needed.
Many tiny payments — airtime, tea sugar, a bus fare — get lost. Keep them in a small separate 'petty cash' tin and book.
A small fixed amount kept aside only for little everyday costs, so you do not dip into the sales drawer.

manas.q: What is petty cash?

children.note: Start with a fixed amount, say 2,000. When it runs low, top it up by exactly what was spent, so it is back to 2,000.

manas.q: What is the imprest (float) system?

children.note: Float 2,000. Spent: tea sugar 150, bus fare 300, soap 250, airtime 400, nails 100 = 1,200. Left in tin: 800.
Put back 1,200 (the amount spent) from the main cash. The tin is back to 2,000 and the main cash book shows 1,200 money out for small costs.
Write a small note for each petty payment: date, what, how much, who. Notes + money left should always equal the float.

manas.q: What should petty cash slips plus cash left add up to?

children.note: Beginners make the same few mistakes. Avoid these and your cash book will almost always balance.
Using the drawer for school fees without writing it down. Always write 'Owner took' when you take money.
Memory fails by evening. Write each sale or payment as it happens, or at least every few hours.
Taking cash to the bank is moving money, not earning it. Record it out of cash and into bank.
Starting a new page at zero instead of bringing down yesterday's closing balance. Every page starts with the balance brought down.
Small fees add up and the M-Pesa column drifts from the real balance. Record every charge.
Erasing or tearing pages looks like hiding things. Draw one line through the error and write the right figure beside it.
Check each week with the formula: opening + in − out = closing. If it disagrees, re-add line by line.
Keep it safe and dry. Kenyan law says business records must be kept for five years after the period ends (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule).

manas.q: How long must Kenyan business records be kept?

children.note: Short practice questions. Work them out first, then open the answer steps.
Opening cash 1,500. Sales 4,000. Paid supplier 2,200. What is the closing cash?
5,500 − 2,200 = 3,300 closing cash, carried down to tomorrow.
The cash column says 9,750. The drawer count is 9,600. What is the difference?
Book 9,750 is more than the drawer 9,600.
9,750 − 9,600 = 150 cash short. Count again, then look for the cause.
Opening M-Pesa 2,000. Received 3,500 and 1,200. Sent 4,000 to a supplier. What is the closing M-Pesa balance?
6,700 − 4,000 = 2,700 closing M-Pesa balance.
You take 5,000 cash to the bank. How does it go in the cash book?
Cash column: 5,000 money out. Bank column: 5,000 money in. Total money is unchanged.

nodeData.note: Every sale, purchase and payment leaves a piece of paper or a message behind. This map shows the everyday business papers, what each one proves, and how to keep them safe so your cash book can be trusted.

children.note: A paper (or SMS or e-invoice) is the proof that something happened. Your cash book from map 2 is only as good as the papers behind it.
A document shows who, what, when and how much. Without it, a figure in your book is just your word.

manas.q: What is a source document?

children.topic: The paper comes first, the book second
children.note: First you get or give the paper, then you write the line in your cash book. Never the other way round.

manas.q: Which comes first: the document or the entry in the book?

children.note: You, your partners, your bank or SACCO when you ask for a loan, the taxman (KRA), and an accountant or auditor checking your books.
A printed receipt, a PDF invoice, an eTIMS invoice and an M-Pesa SMS are all documents. What matters is that they are clear and kept.
Most sales follow the same steps. Each step has its own paper. Follow Baraka Hardware selling chairs to Neema Salon.
Before buying, the customer asks 'how much?'. The seller writes a quotation listing items and prices. It is an offer, not a sale yet.

manas.q: What is a quotation?

children.note: The customer agrees, often with a written order (a purchase order, LPO in Kenya) or a simple message. Now there is a deal.
A delivery note travels with the goods. The customer counts them and signs to show they were received in good condition.

manas.q: What does a signed delivery note prove?

children.note: The seller sends an invoice saying what was sold and how much is owed. It asks for money; it does not show money was paid.

manas.q: What is an invoice?

children.note: When the customer pays, the seller gives a receipt. The receipt proves the money was received.

manas.q: What is a receipt?

children.topic: Fixing mistakes: credit and debit notes
children.note: If goods come back or the price was too high, a credit note cuts the bill. If the bill was too low, a debit note adds to it.
These two get mixed up the most. Simple test: an invoice says 'you owe me', a receipt says 'you have paid me'.
Issued when you sell on credit (pay later). The customer now owes you. Nothing has come into your cash book yet.

manas.q: When is an invoice issued?

children.note: Issued when cash, M-Pesa or a cheque is received. This is the moment money comes in and the cash book gets a line.

manas.q: When is a receipt issued?

children.topic: Cash sale: one paper can do both
children.note: In Mama Wanjiku's duka, the customer pays at once. The till slip or cash sale receipt shows both the sale and the payment.

children.topic: Credit sale: two papers, two dates
children.note: A hotel buys maize flour on 1 May and pays on 31 May. The invoice is dated 1 May; the receipt is dated 31 May.

children.topic: Which goes in the cash book?
children.note: Only the receipt side (real money in or out). The invoice is recorded as money owed until it is paid. Map 4 explains why profit and cash differ.
When money leaves the business you also need proof, signed by the right person.
A form filled before or when paying a bill: who is paid, how much, what for, who approved it. Attach the supplier's invoice to it.

manas.q: What is a payment voucher?

children.topic: Why a voucher, not just an invoice?
children.note: The invoice shows what the supplier wants. The voucher shows the business checked it and a named person agreed to pay.
A small fixed amount of cash kept for tiny costs like milk, tea or a boda boda delivery. It is topped back up to the same amount.

manas.q: What is petty cash?

children.note: A small slip filled for every petty cash spend: date, amount, reason, who took the money, who approved. Staple the shop receipt to it.

manas.q: What is a petty cash voucher?

children.note: A note from the seller that reduces what you owe, for returned or faulty goods, an overcharge or an agreed discount.

manas.q: What is a credit note?

children.topic: Debit note (from the buyer or seller)
children.note: A note that shows an amount should go up, or a buyer's written claim to the seller (for example 'we returned 2 items, please credit us').

manas.q: What is a debit note?

children.note: In Kenya, much of the proof is now on a phone. Know what an M-Pesa message proves and what eTIMS asks of every business.

children.topic: M-Pesa message as proof of payment
children.note: The confirmation SMS shows the transaction code, amount, who paid or was paid, date and time, and the balance. Keep it or screenshot it.

manas.q: What does an M-Pesa confirmation message show?

children.topic: M-Pesa proves money, not what was bought
children.note: The SMS proves payment only. Write on it, or pair it with, an invoice or receipt saying what the money was for.

children.topic: Match the code in your cash book
children.note: Write the M-Pesa transaction code next to the cash book line. Later you can tick it off against your M-Pesa statement (CA11 map 10).
eTIMS is KRA's free electronic Tax Invoice Management System. It runs on a phone or a computer and produces electronic tax invoices. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: What is eTIMS?

children.note: Everyone in business must sign up and issue electronic tax invoices, VAT-registered or not, including sole traders, the informal sector, hospitals and schools. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: Who must issue eTIMS invoices?

children.topic: No eTIMS invoice, no expense claim
children.note: Since 1 January 2024, a business cost can only be claimed for tax if it is backed by an electronic tax invoice. So ask suppliers for one. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

children.topic: Small sellers: the buyer issues it
children.note: If the seller is a small business or small farmer with yearly sales of KES 5 million or less, the buyer makes the invoice for them on eCitizen (Buyer Initiated Invoicing). (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: What is Buyer Initiated Invoicing?

children.topic: Costs that need no eTIMS invoice
children.note: Salaries and wages, imports, air tickets, investment allowances, interest, bank fees, costs under final withholding tax, and services from non-residents with no base in Kenya. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

children.topic: A good invoice and good filing
children.note: A clear invoice gets paid faster and stands up to questions. Good filing means you can find any paper in a minute.
Seller's name, address and KRA PIN; the word 'Invoice'; its own number; date; customer's name; each item, quantity, price and line total; grand total; payment terms.

manas.q: What must a good invoice show?

children.note: Tell the customer when and how to pay, e.g. 'Pay within 30 days to M-Pesa Till or bank account'.
Use one unbroken series (INV-001, INV-002 …). A gap shows at once if a paper is lost or removed.

manas.q: Why do documents have running numbers?

children.topic: Never tear out or reuse a number
children.note: If you spoil an invoice, write 'CANCELLED' across it and keep it. Never throw it away or use the number again.
One file or folder per type (sales invoices, receipts, payment vouchers, petty cash), in number or date order, one for each month.
Save PDFs and screenshots in one named folder and keep a copy elsewhere (cloud or another phone). Phones get lost.
Kenyan law (Section 23, Tax Procedures Act 2015) says keep business and tax records for five years from the end of the period they cover. (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule)

manas.q: How long must Kenyan business records be kept?

children.topic: ✍️ Worked example: invoice and credit note
children.note: Baraka Hardware sells chairs and mirrors to Neema Salon. Follow the numbers from quote to final payment. VAT is not shown, to keep the sums simple.
4 salon chairs × KES 6,500 = KES 26,000. 2 mirrors × KES 3,250 = KES 6,500. Total offered: KES 32,500. Neema says yes.
Neema counts 4 chairs and 2 mirrors and signs. But one mirror is cracked, so she writes 'one mirror cracked' on the note.
Lines: chairs KES 26,000 + mirrors KES 6,500 = KES 32,500. Terms: pay within 30 days. Neema's records now show she owes Baraka KES 32,500.
The cracked mirror goes back. Baraka issues credit note CN-005 for 1 mirror × KES 3,250, quoting INV-087. The bill drops by KES 3,250.
KES 32,500 − KES 3,250 = KES 29,250. This is what Neema now really owes.
Neema pays KES 20,000 by M-Pesa. Baraka gives receipt RC-112 and writes the M-Pesa code on it. Still owing: 29,250 − 20,000 = KES 9,250.
Neema pays the last KES 9,250. Receipt RC-118. Check: 20,000 + 9,250 = 29,250 = invoice 32,500 − credit note 3,250. Fully paid.
Neema Salon keeps a petty cash box of KES 5,000. Each spend gets a petty cash voucher.
On Monday the box is counted and holds KES 5,000. This fixed amount is called the float.
PCV-1 milk and tea KES 350. PCV-2 boda boda delivery KES 1,200. PCV-3 receipt books and pens KES 800. Total spent: KES 2,350.
KES 5,000 − KES 2,350 = KES 2,650 should be left. Count the cash. Cash left plus the vouchers must equal KES 5,000.
The owner gives exactly KES 2,350 back into the box, using the vouchers as proof. The box is back to KES 5,000.
Lost or false papers are how money disappears. Learn the warning signs.
INV-041 then INV-043? Find INV-042. It may be lost, spoiled or hidden on purpose.
Crossed-out or overwritten amounts, different ink, or a total that does not match the lines. Add the lines yourself.

manas.q: Name three signs of a fake document.

children.topic: No name, no PIN, no date
children.note: A 'receipt' on plain paper with only an amount proves almost nothing. Ask for a proper receipt or eTIMS invoice.
A supplier sends a copy and it is paid again. Mark every paid invoice 'PAID', with the date and voucher number.
Fake SMS messages are sent to trick sellers. Check the payment really shows in your own M-Pesa balance or statement before handing over goods.

children.topic: A missing paper: what to do
children.note: Ask the other side for a copy at once. If none exists, write a note of what happened, sign it, and get it approved.
These slips cause most beginner problems.

children.topic: Treating an invoice as a payment
children.note: Sending an invoice does not put money in the bank. Record cash only when a receipt is issued.
Small receipts add up to big sums over a year. Keep them all, stapled to their vouchers.

children.topic: Credit note with no invoice number
children.note: A credit note must say which invoice it reduces. Otherwise nobody knows which bill changed.
Never pay without an approved payment voucher and a real invoice behind it.
Try each question first, then open its bubble to see the steps.

children.topic: Q1: Which paper for a credit sale?
children.note: A matatu owner buys 2 tyres from a garage, to pay next week. What does the garage issue now, and what later?
Now: an invoice (money owed). Next week, when paid: a receipt (money received).
A duka is invoiced KES 18,000 for goods and returns goods worth KES 4,500. What paper does the supplier send, and what is owed?
The supplier sends a credit note for KES 4,500, quoting the invoice number.
KES 18,000 − KES 4,500 = KES 13,500 still owed.
A float of KES 3,000. Vouchers: KES 450, KES 900 and KES 1,150. How much should be in the box, and what is the top-up?
Box: 3,000 − 2,500 = KES 500. Top-up: KES 2,500, bringing it back to KES 3,000.

maps.title: 4. Profit is not the same as cash

nodeData.topic: Profit is not the same as cash
nodeData.note: A business can make a profit and still have no money, or make a loss with a full till. This map shows why, with one month of a duka worked out both ways.

children.note: Two different questions about a business. Profit asks "did I earn more than it cost me?" Cash asks "how much money do I actually have right now?"
Profit = sales minus the costs of making those sales. If sales are bigger, you made a profit; if costs are bigger, you made a loss.

manas.q: What is profit?

children.note: The value of everything you sold in the period, whether the customer paid you today or will pay later.

manas.q: Do sales count only when the customer pays?

children.note: What it cost you to earn those sales: the stock you sold, rent, wages, power, and a share of things used up.
When costs are bigger than sales. A loss of KES 15,000 means the month cost you KES 15,000 more than it earned.
Cash is the money you can spend now: notes and coins in the till, plus money in M-Pesa and the bank.

manas.q: What counts as cash?

children.note: Your cash book from topic 2 shows it: money that came in minus money that went out tells you how your cash changed.

children.topic: Profit is a score, cash is fuel
children.note: Profit tells you if the business is worth running. Cash keeps it running today. You need both.

manas.q: Why do you need both profit and cash?

children.topic: Why the same month gives two answers
children.note: Profit counts what you earned and used up. Cash counts when money actually moved. These often happen in different months.
Six everyday reasons why profit and cash do not match. Learn them and the puzzle goes away.
You sell KES 30,000 to a customer who will pay next month. It is a sale (profit goes up) but no cash came in yet.

manas.q: How does selling on credit affect profit and cash?

children.note: When last month's customer pays you today, cash goes up but profit does not. The sale was already counted last month.
Stock on your shelf is still yours. It becomes a cost only when you sell it. Buying KES 110,000 of stock and selling KES 90,000 worth means KES 20,000 of cash sits on the shelf.

manas.q: When does stock become a cost?

children.note: A fridge or a motorbike lasts years. You pay all the cash today, but only a small share of its cost goes into each month's profit as it wears out.

manas.q: Why is equipment not a full cost in the month you buy it?

children.note: The small monthly share of equipment cost charged against profit. No cash moves for it, because you already paid for the item.

manas.q: What is depreciation, in everyday words?

children.note: A SACCO loan brings cash in, but it is not a sale, so profit does not change. Paying the loan back takes cash out but is not a cost. Only the interest is a cost.

manas.q: Does a loan received count as profit?

children.note: Money the owner takes for home, like school fees. Cash goes down, but it is not a business cost, so profit does not change.

manas.q: What are owner drawings?

children.note: Paying 12 months of insurance now, KES 12,000. Cash goes down by the full amount today, but each month's profit carries only KES 1,000.

manas.q: What is a prepayment?

children.note: If you used power this month but pay the bill next month, profit already carries the cost but cash has not left yet. This is called an accrual.
A business can make money and still run dry, or lose money and feel rich. Real numbers make this clear.

children.topic: Story 1: profitable but out of cash
children.note: Otieno supplies school uniforms. Big orders, good profit, but the schools pay after 60 days.
Sales to schools KES 500,000 on credit. Cloth and tailoring KES 350,000 paid cash. Rent and wages KES 40,000 paid. Profit = 500,000 − 350,000 − 40,000 = KES 110,000.
He started with KES 300,000. Cash out was 350,000 + 40,000 = 390,000 and nothing came in. He is KES 90,000 short.
Growing fast on credit eats cash. Profit on paper cannot pay the landlord. Many businesses close this way.

manas.q: How can a profitable business fail?

children.note: Mama Wanjiku's duka in April, the month after the worked example below.
Cash sales KES 80,000. Stock sold cost KES 70,000. Rent, wages and power KES 25,000. Profit = 80,000 − 70,000 − 25,000 = a loss of KES 15,000.
She sold stock already bought in March, and only bought KES 20,000 new. A customer also paid an old KES 30,000 debt.
Cash in = 80,000 + 30,000 = 110,000. Cash out = 20,000 + 25,000 = 45,000. Cash went UP by KES 65,000 in a loss month.
A full till does not mean the business is doing well. Check profit too, or you may spend money you need to restock.

manas.q: Can a business have more cash in a month it makes a loss?

children.note: One month (March) of a small duka, worked out twice: once for profit and once for cash. Then we join the two.

Cash sales 120,000. Credit sales 30,000. Old debt collected 8,000. Stock bought 110,000, sold stock that cost 90,000. Rent 10,000, wages 15,000, power 2,000. Fridge 40,000. Insurance for a year 12,000. SACCO loan 50,000 in, old loan 5,000 repaid. She took 12,000 for school fees. All KES.
Work out what she earned and what it cost her.
Cash sales 120,000 + credit sales 30,000 = KES 150,000.
Only the stock she sold: KES 90,000. Sales minus this = 60,000 (gross profit).
Rent 10,000 + wages 15,000 + power 2,000 + one month of insurance 1,000 + fridge wear 1,000 = KES 29,000.
60,000 − 29,000 = KES 31,000 profit. A good month.
Count only money that really came in or went out.
Cash sales 120,000 + old debt 8,000 + SACCO loan 50,000 = KES 178,000.
Stock 110,000 + rent 10,000 + wages 15,000 + power 2,000 + insurance 12,000 + fridge 40,000 + loan repaid 5,000 + school fees 12,000 = KES 206,000.
178,000 − 206,000 = cash DOWN by KES 28,000. She began with 40,000 and ends with 12,000.

children.topic: Joining them: from profit to cash
children.note: Start with profit and adjust for each difference. You must land exactly on the cash change.

manas.q: How do you get from profit to the change in cash?

children.note: +1,000 (a cost with no cash). Running total 32,000.
−30,000 (sold, not yet paid). Total 2,000.
+8,000 (cash with no new sale). Total 10,000.

children.topic: Take off extra stock on shelf

children.note: −12,000. Total −28,000: exactly the cash change. It balances.
A good profit of 31,000, but cash fell 28,000. The fridge, extra stock and credit customers ate the cash, and the loan helped cover it.
Simple habits that keep money in the till while the business grows.
Write down every credit sale, agree a pay date, and follow up kindly but firmly. Money owed is not money you can spend.

manas.q: Why should you chase debts quickly?

children.note: Give credit only to trusted customers and set a limit, such as KES 5,000 each.
Buy what sells. Slow stock ties up cash and may expire or spoil.

manas.q: Why is overstocking bad for cash?

children.note: Save for equipment, or use a loan you can repay from the extra profit it brings.
Use a separate M-Pesa line, till or bank account for the business. Pay yourself a fixed amount instead of dipping into the till.

manas.q: Why keep home and business money apart?

children.note: Every shilling you take home goes in the cash book as drawings, so you know the true picture.
List the money you expect in and out for the next few weeks. You will see a shortfall before it happens.
KRA lets a business expense count for tax only when backed by an eTIMS electronic tax invoice (checked 19 Nov 2026 — check the current KRA rule).
Traps that catch new business owners and new students.
Wrong. The till includes loans, old debts and money not yet spent on costs you owe.
A loan must be paid back. It is not a sale and never part of profit.
School fees taken from the till lower cash, not profit. Treat them as the owner taking money out.

children.topic: Charging all of the equipment at once
children.note: Putting the whole 40,000 fridge into one month makes that month look like a loss. Spread it over its life.
If you count only cash sales, you understate what you earned.
Bought stock is not a cost until sold. Count your stock at month end.
Short questions. Try them, then open the answer steps.
A salon does KES 20,000 of hair for a wedding, paid next month. What happens to profit and cash this month?
Profit goes up by 20,000 (the work is done). Cash does not change until the customer pays.
Fares 45,000, fuel and repairs 20,000, takes 10,000 home, repays 8,000 of bike loan. Profit? Cash change?
45,000 − 20,000 = KES 25,000. Drawings and loan repayment are not costs.
Give two possible reasons.
For example: customers still owe money from credit sales, or she bought equipment or extra stock. Drawings or loan repayments also take cash.

maps.title: 5. Your own budget and household accounts

nodeData.topic: Your own budget and household accounts
nodeData.note: A budget is a simple money plan for your home: what will come in, and where it will go, before the month starts. This map shows how to make one, check it, and save. It is general education, not financial advice.

children.note: Start here: the idea of a budget and why a family needs one.
A budget is a list made before the month: money you expect in, and how you will use it. It tells your money where to go, instead of wondering where it went.

manas.q: What is a budget?

children.note: The cash book (map 2) records what really happened. The budget is the plan made in advance. Put them side by side to learn.

manas.q: How is a budget different from a cash book?

children.note: A budget stops month-end surprises, shows where money leaks, and helps you save for school fees, emergencies and goals.
Everyone with money coming in: a salaried worker, a boda boda rider paid daily, a student with pocket money, a family.
Most homes plan for one month, because rent and salary come monthly. If you are paid daily, plan by week and add up four weeks.

children.topic: Two lists: money in and money out
children.note: Every budget has an income list and a spending list.
All money you expect this month: salary, business money taken home, rent from a room, money from family. Write only money you are fairly sure of.

manas.q: What goes on the income list?

children.note: Everything you plan to pay: rent, food, fares, fees, airtime, savings, loan repayments, treats. Group small items so the list stays short.
If income goes up and down, use a careful (low) figure for money in and a full figure for money out. Surprises are then good ones.
Money left over = total income minus total planned spending. If it is below zero, cut something before the month starts.

manas.q: How do you find money left in a budget?

children.note: Some costs come once a term or year, like school fees. Divide the yearly cost by 12 and set that amount aside each month.

manas.q: How do you budget for a cost that comes once a year?

children.note: Two simple ways to sort the spending list: needs vs wants, and fixed vs changing costs.
Things you must have to live and work: shelter, basic food, water, fares to work, school fees, repaying what you owe.

manas.q: What is a need?

children.note: Things that make life nicer but you can live without for a while: eating out, new clothes, outings, extra data bundles.

manas.q: What is a want?

children.note: Some items are part need, part want. Basic phone credit may be a need; a big data bundle for videos is a want. Be honest with yourself.
Costs that stay the same each month, such as rent, a set chama contribution or a fixed loan repayment.

manas.q: What is a fixed cost in a household budget?

children.note: Costs that go up and down: food, fares, electricity tokens, airtime. These are where most overspending happens.

manas.q: What is a changing (variable) cost?

children.note: When money is short, reduce wants and changing costs first. Fixed needs like rent are hard to change quickly.
The Otieno family in Nairobi plans November. All amounts are made-up teaching numbers.
Salary (Otieno) 42,000; Salon money brought home (Akinyi) 13,000. Total income = KES 55,000.
Chama 3,000; Emergency fund 2,500. Saving total = KES 5,500. This is paid on the day money arrives.
Rent 12,000; Food 14,000; School fees set aside 6,000; Matatu fares 4,500; Electricity tokens 1,500; Water 800; Loan repayment 3,000. Needs total = KES 41,800.
Airtime and data 1,200; Giving 1,000; Clothes 1,000; Outings and treats 1,500; Other small things 2,000. Total = KES 6,700.
Saving 5,500 + needs 41,800 + wants 6,700 = KES 54,000 planned spending.
Income 55,000 minus planned spending 54,000 = KES 1,000 left as a small cushion.
Fixed (chama, emergency fund, rent, school fees, loan, giving) = KES 27,500. Changing (all the rest) = KES 26,500. 27,500 + 26,500 = 54,000.
At month end, compare the plan with what really happened. The gap is called the difference (variance).
Actual is what you really received and spent, taken from your cash book, receipts and M-Pesa statement.

manas.q: What is the "actual" in budget vs actual?

children.note: Difference = actual minus budget. For spending, a plus figure means you spent more than planned (overspent); a minus figure means you spent less.

manas.q: How do you work out the difference between budget and actual?

children.note: Food 14,000 → 15,800 (+1,800); Matatu fares 4,500 → 5,100 (+600); Electricity tokens 1,500 → 1,350 (-150); Airtime and data 1,200 → 1,650 (+450); Outings and treats 1,500 → 2,700 (+1,200); Other small things 2,000 → 1,400 (-600).
Overspent 4,050 − underspent 750 = KES 3,300 over budget. Actual spending KES 57,300 (54,000 + 3,300).
Income 55,000 − actual 57,300 = −2,300. Overspending of 3,300 = the 1,000 cushion + KES 2,300 taken from the emergency fund.
Food and outings caused most of the gap. Next month: a shopping list, a weekly food limit, and one outing instead of three.
Comparing every month is what makes a budget work. After three months, your plan becomes much closer to real life.
Pay yourself first, then keep a safety cushion for bad days.
Move your saving out on the day money arrives, then live on the rest. Money 'left at month end' is usually zero.

manas.q: What does "pay yourself first" mean?

children.note: Money kept aside only for real emergencies, such as a hospital visit, a job loss or a broken phone needed for work. It stops you borrowing in a panic.

manas.q: What is an emergency fund?

children.note: A common aim is a few months of needs. For the Otienos, 3 months × 41,800 = KES 125,400. That is big, so start with a small first goal.
First goal KES 10,000. At 2,500 a month: 10,000 ÷ 2,500 = 4 months.
Keep the fund separate from spending money, for example in a separate savings account, so it is not used for treats.
If you use the fund, as the Otienos did, make refilling it part of next month's budget.
Group saving is a strong habit in Kenya. Here we look only at the habit, not at any product.
A chama is a group of people who agree to save together regularly. In some, members take turns to receive the pot (a merry-go-round).

manas.q: What is a chama?

children.note: A SACCO (savings and credit cooperative) is a member-owned body where members save and can borrow from the group's savings.

manas.q: What is a SACCO?

children.note: A fixed date and friends who expect you make saving a habit. It works like a fixed cost in your budget.
Put the contribution in the budget as a fixed line, paid first. Do not join more groups than your budget can carry.
Write every contribution and every payout in your own book or phone notes, and check them against the group's records.
Ask how records are kept, who signs for money, and what happens if someone leaves. Choosing a group is your own decision.
Much of today's spending happens on the phone, so the phone statement is part of your household accounts.
Many small sends and Buy Goods payments feel like nothing, but together they can be a large part of the month.
M-Pesa can give you a statement listing every transaction. Read it once a week.
Mark each line with a budget heading: food, fares, airtime, family, bills. Then add each heading.
Buy Goods at the shop 2,350; Pay Bill for electricity tokens 1,350; Send money to mum 1,000; Cash withdrawn at agent 2,000; Airtime bought 400. Total = KES 7,100 for the week.
Sending and withdrawing usually carry small charges. They are shown on the statement; add them to your 'other small things' line.
Cash taken out at an agent disappears from the statement. Write down what the cash was spent on, or it becomes 'unknown'.
Debt is not always bad, but it must fit your budget.

children.topic: Borrow only what you can repay
children.note: Before borrowing, check that the repayment fits inside your monthly money left. If it does not, do not borrow.

manas.q: What is the golden rule of borrowing?

children.topic: You repay more than you borrow
children.note: Lenders charge for lending (interest and fees). So the total paid back is always more than the amount borrowed.

manas.q: Why do you repay more than you borrow?

children.note: Illustrative example only, not a real rate: borrow KES 10,000 and repay KES 11,000. The extra KES 1,000 is the cost of the loan.
The Otienos have KES 1,000 left each month. A loan needing 11,000 next month does not fit, so they should not take it.
Quick loans on the phone are easy to take and easy to forget. Write each one in your budget the day you take it.
Once you owe money, the repayment becomes a fixed need in the budget, ahead of wants.
If you run a duka, salon or boda boda, keep the home purse and the business purse apart.
Use separate money for the business and the home: a separate till, wallet, or M-Pesa line for the business.

manas.q: Why keep home and business money separate?

children.note: She takes cash from the duka drawer for home food without writing it down. At week end, the shop cash looks short and she cannot tell her profit.
Better: take a fixed amount each week from the business for home, and record it as money taken out by the owner (drawings).

manas.q: What are drawings?

children.note: Duka sales in the week KES 30,000. She records KES 4,000 taken for home. The cash book now explains the cash, and her home budget shows 4,000 coming in.
Mixed money hides whether the business really makes a profit (map 4) and makes the home budget unreliable.
Traps that break most first budgets.
School fees, a wedding gift or a phone repair are forgotten, then cause a crisis. Set aside a monthly share.
Waiting to save 'what is left' usually means saving nothing. Save first.
A plan that is never compared with real spending is just a wish list.
A budget with no room for treats is hard to keep. Allow a small amount for wants.
Do not spend expected money (a promised payment) before it arrives.
Using shop cash for home without recording it hides both the profit and the true home spending.
Try each one, then open the answer bubbles.
Find the money left.
What is the difference, and is it good or bad?
11,200 − 10,000 = +KES 1,200. Spending more than planned means overspent.
Which is fixed and which is changing?
Rent is fixed (same each month). Electricity tokens are changing (depend on use).
You save KES 2,500 a month. How many months to reach KES 30,000?

children.note: Accounting has its own words. Learn them a few at a time, in this order, and the later topics will feel much easier.
Each bubble gives the plain meaning first and the accounting word second, like "what you own (assets)".
Most words come with a tiny Kenyan example, such as a duka, a matatu or M-Pesa.
The brackets tell you which later topic explains the word fully, for example (CA11 · 3 Double entry).
Many bubbles are flashcards. Read the question, say your answer out loud, then open the note.
These words describe what a business has, what it owes, and what belongs to the owner.
Something the business owns or controls that will bring money or use later. A duka's shelves, stock and M-Pesa balance are assets.

manas.q: What is an asset?

children.note: Money or goods the business must hand over to someone else later. A SACCO loan or an unpaid supplier bill is a liability.

manas.q: What is a liability?

children.note: The part of the business that belongs to the owner: what is left after taking what is owed away from what is owned. (CA11 · 2 The accounting equation)

manas.q: What is capital (owner's equity)?

children.note: Money or goods the owner takes out of the business for personal use. Taking KES 5,000 from the till for school fees is drawings, not an expense.
A person or business that owes you money, usually because you sold on credit. A hotel that took 20 crates of soda and will pay next week is a debtor.

manas.q: Who is a debtor (receivable)?

children.note: A person or business you owe money to, usually because you bought on credit. The wholesaler who gave you flour to pay at month end is a creditor.

manas.q: Who is a creditor (payable)?

children.note: Goods kept to sell, or materials to make things to sell. Sugar, soap and bread on a duka's shelves are stock. (IAS 2 Inventories, later papers)
Something kept and used for more than a year, not for selling. A matatu, a fridge or a building.
Something that will turn into cash or be used up within a year: cash, M-Pesa balance, stock, debtors.
Money borrowed that must be paid back, usually with interest. It is a liability, not income.
These words describe money earned, money spent and what is left.
Money the business earns from its normal work, such as sales or fees. A matatu's daily fares are revenue.

manas.q: What is revenue (income)?

children.note: Sales are what you sell. Turnover is the total sales for a period, for example a month or a year. Turnover is not profit.

manas.q: What does turnover mean?

children.note: Money used up to run the business for a period: rent, wages, fuel, airtime. It reduces profit.

manas.q: What is an expense?

children.note: What the goods you sold cost you to buy or make. If you sold bread you bought for KES 50 a loaf, the KES 50 per loaf is cost of sales.
What is left when expenses are smaller than income for a period. (Start here · 4 Profit is not the same as cash)

manas.q: What is profit?

children.note: What happens when expenses are bigger than income for a period. A loss reduces the owner's capital.
The actual cash and M-Pesa money moving in and out over a period. A business can show profit and still run short of cash.

manas.q: What is cash flow?

children.note: A cash sale is paid at once (cash or M-Pesa). A credit sale is paid later, so it creates a debtor.
A reduction in price. A trade discount is a lower price for a big buyer; a cash discount is a reward for paying early.
The extra money paid for borrowing, or earned for lending or saving. Interest on a SACCO loan is an expense.
Words for the records where transactions are written down. (CA11 · 3 Double entry)
Any event that changes the business's money or things: a sale, a purchase, paying rent.
The paper or message that proves a transaction happened: receipt, invoice, M-Pesa SMS. (Start here · 3 Receipts, invoices and vouchers)
A diary where each transaction is first written, in date order, showing which accounts change. (CA11 · 3 Double entry)

manas.q: What is a journal?

children.note: A book or file with a separate page (an "account") for each thing, such as Cash, Sales or Rent.

manas.q: What is a ledger?

children.note: One page of the ledger that collects everything about one item, for example the "Rent" account.
The left side of an account. Increases in assets and expenses are written on the debit side. It does not mean "bad".

manas.q: What is a debit?

children.note: The right side of an account. Increases in liabilities, capital and income are written on the credit side. It does not mean "good".

manas.q: What is a credit?

children.note: Every transaction is written twice, once as a debit and once as a credit of the same amount, so the books always balance.

manas.q: What is double entry?

children.note: The difference between the two sides of an account. "Cash has a debit balance of KES 30,000" means KES 30,000 is there.
The book that records all cash and bank (and often M-Pesa) money in and out. (Start here · 2 Money in, money out)
A small float of cash kept for tiny daily costs like tea, matatu fare or a padlock.
Copying entries from the journal or cash book into the ledger accounts.
Words for the summaries made from the books at the end of a period.
A list of all account balances, debits in one column and credits in the other. If the totals match, the arithmetic is probably right. (CA11 · 4 Trial balance)

manas.q: What is a trial balance?

children.note: A report of income minus expenses for a period, showing profit or loss.

manas.q: What does an income statement show?

children.note: A snapshot on one day of what the business owns, owes and the owner's capital.

manas.q: What does a balance sheet show?

children.note: A report of where cash came from and where it went during the period.
The set of final reports: income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement and notes.
The length of time a report covers, usually one year, sometimes a month or a quarter.
Spreading the cost of a long-life asset over the years it is used. A KES 600,000 machine used for 6 years might be charged about KES 100,000 a year. (IAS 16, later papers)

manas.q: What is depreciation?

children.note: Counting income or an expense in the period it belongs to, even if cash moves later. December's unpaid electricity bill still belongs to December.

manas.q: What is an accrual?

children.note: Paying now for something you will use later. Rent paid in advance for next month is a prepayment, an asset for now.
Money a customer owes that you no longer expect to get. It is written off as an expense.
A plan of expected income and spending for a future period. (Start here · 5 Your own budget)
Words you will meet running a business in Kenya. Rates change, so always check the current KRA rate.
Kenya Revenue Authority: the government body that collects taxes.
Your tax number. You need it to register a business, open many accounts and file returns.
Value Added Tax: a tax added to the price of many goods and services, collected by registered businesses and paid to KRA. Check the current KRA rate.

manas.q: What is VAT?

children.note: Pay As You Earn: income tax taken from an employee's salary by the employer and sent to KRA. Check the current KRA rates.

manas.q: What is PAYE?

children.note: Besides PAYE, employers take other statutory deductions from pay, such as social security and health contributions. Check the current rules.
KRA's electronic invoicing system. Many businesses must issue invoices through it so KRA can see sales. Check KRA's current guidance.
The form you file with KRA each year (or month for some taxes) showing income and tax due, usually on iTax.
An independent check of the books and reports by a qualified auditor, who gives an opinion on whether they are fair. (Step 3 · Audit papers)
KASNEB sets and runs the CPA exams. ICPAK is the professional body that licenses accountants in Kenya.
Words beginners often mix up. Learn them side by side.
Gross means before taking something off; net means after. Gross profit is sales minus cost of sales; net profit is after all other expenses too.

manas.q: What is the difference between gross and net?

children.note: Profit is income minus expenses. Cash is money you actually hold. Credit sales make profit before cash comes in.
A debtor owes you (an asset). A creditor is owed by you (a liability).
Revenue spending is for day-to-day running (fuel). Capital spending buys long-life assets (a new matatu).
An expense is spent for the business. Drawings are taken by the owner for personal use. Only expenses reduce profit.
An invoice asks to be paid. A receipt shows payment has been made. (Start here · 3 Receipts, invoices and vouchers)

manas.q: What is the difference between an invoice and a receipt?

children.note: Turnover is total sales. Profit is what is left after costs. Big turnover can still mean a loss.
Bookkeeping is recording transactions. Accounting also summarises, explains and uses those records to make decisions.
Mama Wanjiru's duka on 31 December. All figures in KES. This shows the words working together.
Wholesaler (creditor) 40,000 + SACCO loan 60,000 = 100,000.
Capital = assets 220,000 − liabilities 100,000 = 120,000.
Assets 220,000 = liabilities 100,000 + capital 120,000. Both sides equal 220,000.

manas.q: State the accounting equation.

children.note: Sales 50,000 − cost of sales 30,000 = gross profit 20,000. Less rent 8,000 and wages 5,000 = net profit 7,000.
Do not count the SACCO loan as income, or her drawings as an expense. Both would give a wrong profit.

nodeData.note: Accounting began with notches and clay tokens, grew into double entry in Italy, became a profession in the 1800s and is now global and digital. This is that story, ending in Kenya today.

children.note: Knowing where accounting came from makes the rules feel less strange. Each idea was invented to solve a real problem: remembering debts, stopping theft, or showing owners the truth.
People needed to remember who owed what, check stores of grain and collect taxes. Accounting grew out of those everyday needs.
Words like debit, credit, ledger, journal and audit come from this long history. Learning their roots helps them stick.
A notched stick, a clay tablet, a paper ledger and an app on a phone all do one job: keep an honest record.
Accounting moved from marks on bones to clay, paper, books, rules, computers and phones. Here it is in eight short steps.
Before writing, people kept count with notches and small clay shapes. These were the first records of what was owed or stored.
A stick or bone with cut notches used to remember numbers, goods or debts. It is one of the oldest memory aids.

manas.q: What is a tally stick?

children.note: A notched bone found at Ishango in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from the Old Stone Age. Some think it was a tally stick.

manas.q: Where was the Ishango bone found?

children.note: The stick was notched, then split in two. Each side kept a half; only the true halves fit together, so it worked as proof of a debt.

manas.q: How did a split tally prove a debt?

children.note: King Henry I brought the split tally into the English Exchequer around 1100. It stayed in use there until 1826.
In the ancient Near East, small clay tokens stood for goods. They were sealed inside hollow clay balls (bullae) so nobody could change the count.

manas.q: What were bullae used for?

children.note: Early cities and temples needed to track grain, herds, taxes and stores. Writing and counting grew alongside these records.
Lists of spending, goods received and goods traded have been found in Mesopotamia. They are among the oldest accounts known.

children.topic: Kushim: a name on a receipt
children.note: Kushim is a name on clay tablets recording barley, about 3200 BC. It may be the oldest written name of a person, and it is on an account.
Egypt had a title like "comptroller of the scribes". Egyptians and Babylonians checked goods moving in and out of storehouses.
Early checks were often spoken aloud. The word auditor comes from the Latin audire, to hear.

manas.q: Where does the word "auditor" come from?

children.note: Emperor Augustus kept detailed public accounts of revenue, cash in the treasury and spending. Roman forts like Vindolanda kept daily cash records.
Merchants in South Asia and the Middle East kept careful books long before Europe caught up.
A traditional Indian account book (ledger) used to keep financial records. In 2019 India's Finance Minister carried the budget in one.

manas.q: What is a bahi-khata?

children.note: Islamic teaching asked believers to record debts, and inheritance shares needed careful sums. This pushed scholars to develop record and calculation methods.
The numerals 0–9 came from India through the Arab world. They made adding, dividing and checking far easier than Roman numerals.

manas.q: Why did Hindu-Arabic numerals help bookkeeping?

children.note: Records from the Cairo Geniza show bankers in Cairo using a double-entry style before it is seen in Italy.
Italian merchants and banks made double entry an everyday system, and Pacioli spread it in print.
Liber Abaci taught Italian merchants Hindu-Arabic numerals and business sums. Copies were hand-made, so few people saw it at first.
A Florentine merchant firm's ledger. It is the earliest surviving full double-entry record.

manas.q: What is the earliest surviving full double-entry ledger?

children.note: The treasurer's (Messari) accounts of Genoa used debits, credits and balances brought forward. They are widely accepted as complete double entry.
Benedetto Cotrugli described double entry in a manuscript in 1458, but it was not printed until 1573.
Pacioli, a Franciscan friar and maths teacher, printed a 27-page bookkeeping section in his Summa in Venice. He is called the father of accounting.

manas.q: Who published the first printed book on double entry, and when?

children.note: Memorandum (rough notes), journal (day book) and ledger (accounts), with an index. The ledger was the central book.

manas.q: What three books did Pacioli describe?

children.note: Bigger businesses with distant owners needed more careful accounts, cost figures and independent checks.
Investors owned shares but did not run the business. They relied on accounts, which split reporting into outside (financial) and inside (management) uses.

manas.q: Why did joint-stock companies change accounting?

children.note: Factories and limited companies needed depreciation, stock valuation and company-law know-how. Demand for skilled accountants grew fast.
Railways, steel and big factories had large fixed costs. Owners needed to know what each product really cost, so cost accounting grew.

manas.q: What pushed the growth of cost accounting?

children.note: Outside owners wanted someone independent to check the accounts. This made audit a regular part of company life.
In the 1800s accountants organised into bodies with exams, titles and rules of conduct.
The modern chartered accountant began in Scotland. Glasgow accountants asked Queen Victoria for a royal charter in 1854.

manas.q: Where did the chartered accountant profession begin?

children.note: Local bodies in England joined to form the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales in 1880.
The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants was set up in 1887.
In the 20th century countries wanted company accounts that could be compared across borders.
The International Accounting Standards Committee was set up in June 1973 by accountancy bodies from ten countries. It issued standards called IAS.

manas.q: When was the IASC set up?

children.note: On 1 April 2001 the International Accounting Standards Board took over from the IASC. New standards were named IFRS.

manas.q: What replaced the IASC, and when?

children.note: IFRS let investors compare companies across countries. The USA still uses its own US GAAP; smaller entities often use IFRS for SMEs.

manas.q: What does IFRS stand for?

children.note: The IFRS Foundation added a sister board, the ISSB, in 2021 to set sustainability reporting standards.
Machines took over the adding, so accountants spend more time checking and explaining.
The first spreadsheet program for personal computers, released for the Apple II in 1979. It turned the PC into a business tool.

manas.q: What was the first PC spreadsheet program?

children.note: Software now posts both sides of each entry automatically. Cloud systems let owners and accountants see the same books from anywhere.
Tax authorities, including Kenya's KRA, increasingly ask for invoices sent electronically. Check the current KRA rules for your business.
Kenya has its own exam board, professional body and digital money that shape how books are kept.
The Kenya Accountants and Secretaries National Examinations Board sets the CPA exams in Kenya. Wikipedia notes it was founded in 1969.

manas.q: What does KASNEB do?

children.note: ICPAK regulates the profession under the Accountants Act No. 15 of 2008. It is a member of IFAC and the Pan African Federation of Accountants.

manas.q: Under which law does ICPAK work?

children.note: ICPAK founded the Kenya College of Accountancy in May 1989. It later became KCA University.
The Kenya Revenue Authority began on 1 July 1995. It assesses and collects government revenue.
Safaricom and Vodafone launched M-Pesa in 2007. Each payment leaves a digital record, a modern receipt for small businesses.

children.note: Old methods shown with today's Kenyan shillings, so you can see how little the logic has changed.
A Venetian cloth merchant sells cloth worth KES 45,000 to Marco on credit. Single entry only writes: "Marco owes 45,000". Nothing shows the sale or the stock leaving.
Dr Marco (debtor) KES 45,000 / Cr Sales KES 45,000. One side shows who owes, the other shows what was earned. Debits 45,000 = credits 45,000.
Dr Cash KES 45,000 / Cr Marco (debtor) KES 45,000. Marco's account now nets to zero (45,000 − 45,000).
After both entries: Cash Dr 45,000; Sales Cr 45,000; Marco 0. Total debits 45,000 = total credits 45,000.
The cloth cost the merchant KES 30,000. Profit = 45,000 − 30,000 = KES 15,000.
Memorandum: rough note "sold sugar 2,000 to Wanjiku". Journal: Dr Wanjiku 2,000 / Cr Sales 2,000. Ledger: posted to Wanjiku's and Sales accounts.
A farmer lends KES 5,000; five notches of 1,000 are cut, then the stick split. Lender keeps the stock, borrower the foil; both halves show 5,000.

It helps spot errors, but a wrong entry posted on both sides still balances. That is why audits exist.

He spread double entry widely; he did not invent it.

nodeData.note: Accountants keep the money story of a business, a hospital or a government true and clear. This map shows the jobs, where accountants work, the skills you need, and how to start in Kenya.

children.note: In plain words: an accountant records money coming in and going out, checks it is right, and explains what it means so people can decide well.
Writes down every sale, purchase, payment and receipt in the books or accounting software, the same day if possible.

manas.q: What is bookkeeping?

children.note: Matches the books to the bank statement, M-Pesa statement and supplier statements, and fixes any difference.

manas.q: What is a reconciliation?

children.note: Turns the records into reports such as the profit or loss for the year and what the business owns and owes.
Works out tax the business owes, files returns with KRA on time, and pays staff correctly with the right deductions.
Explains the numbers: which products make money, where costs are rising, whether there is cash to expand.
Sets simple checks so cash is not stolen or wasted, such as two people signing large payments.
Daily: post transactions, chase customers who owe. Weekly: reconcile bank and M-Pesa. Monthly: close the books and report. Yearly: audit and tax return.
Accounting is not one job but a ladder of many. Most people start near the bottom and move up as they qualify and gain experience.
Entry job. Records daily transactions, files invoices and receipts, keeps the cash book up to date.

manas.q: What does a bookkeeper or accounts clerk do?

children.note: Helps the accountant: posts invoices, does bank and M-Pesa reconciliations, prepares schedules for month-end.

manas.q: What does an accounts assistant do?

children.note: Pays staff every month: works out gross pay, deductions such as PAYE, and net pay, then files the payroll returns.

manas.q: What does a payroll officer do?

children.note: Helps businesses and people follow tax law, file returns, claim what they are allowed, and deal with KRA queries.

manas.q: What does a tax consultant do?

children.note: Works for an audit firm and checks a client's financial statements, then gives an independent opinion on whether they are fair.

manas.q: What does an external auditor do?

children.note: Works inside one organisation, testing its controls and processes and reporting weaknesses to management or the board.

manas.q: How is an internal auditor different from an external auditor?

children.note: Looks forward, not back: budgets, product costs, and reports that help managers plan and control the business.

manas.q: What does a management accountant do?

children.note: Prepares the official financial statements for owners, lenders and tax authorities, following accounting standards.

manas.q: What does a financial accountant do?

children.note: Leads the finance team. The Chief Finance Officer (CFO) plans funding, cash and strategy with the top leaders.

manas.q: What is a CFO?

children.note: Investigates fraud and money disputes, traces where money went, and may give evidence in court.

manas.q: What does a forensic accountant do?

children.note: Manages public money in ministries, counties and state agencies, following government budget and reporting rules.
A qualified accountant can run their own firm, serving many small clients with books, tax, advice and, if licensed, audit.
Every organisation that handles money needs accounting, so accountants work almost everywhere.
From the big international firms to small local practices. Good place to learn fast on many clients.
Manufacturers, supermarkets, pharmacy wholesalers, telecoms, transport. Most accountants work in business, not in audit firms.
National ministries, county governments and state corporations need accountants and internal auditors.
Track donor grants carefully and report how every shilling was spent, often to strict donor rules.
Record members' savings and loans, work out interest and dividends, and meet regulator reporting.
Finance, risk, credit and regulatory reporting teams all need accounting skills.
Bill patients and insurers, manage pharmacy stock, pay staff and suppliers, and control costs.
Bookkeeping and tax services for dukas, matatu owners, landlords and small firms; qualified CPAs can open a practice.
You do not need to be a maths genius. You need care, honesty and steady practice.
Adding, percentages and checking totals. Careful and accurate matters more than fast or clever.

manas.q: What level of maths does accounting need?

children.note: People trust your numbers. Never hide a mistake or bend figures to please a boss; ethics is a core part of the CPA.

manas.q: Why are honesty and ethics key for accountants?

children.note: Sums, sorting, filters, simple formulas and pivot tables are used every day in almost every finance job.

manas.q: Which computer tool do accountants use most?

children.note: Learn at least one accounting package and how online tax filing works; employers value hands-on practice.
Explaining numbers simply to non-accountants, writing clear emails and reports, and asking good questions.
Keeping files tidy, meeting deadlines (tax dates, month-end) and following up until things are done.

Meet Wanjiku, an accounts assistant at a pharmacy wholesaler in Nairobi. Her day shows how the jobs above fit together.
She downloads yesterday's bank and M-Pesa statements and marks which customer payments came in.
A hospital pays KES 48,000 into the bank for last month's order. Dr Bank 48,000 / Cr Trade receivables 48,000.
A supplier invoice for medicines arrives: KES 120,000 on credit. Dr Inventory 120,000 / Cr Trade payables 120,000.
The M-Pesa statement is KES 350 lower than her cash book. The difference is transaction charges not yet recorded.
Dr Bank charges (expense) KES 350 / Cr M-Pesa account KES 350. Debits 350 = credits 350, and the two balances now agree.
Cash book was KES 86,350; statement KES 86,000. After the journal: 86,350 − 350 = 86,000. Matched.
She lists overdue customers and sends the reconciliation to her manager for review and sign-off.
